To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the almost-sure winning set of concurrent zero-sum games with qualitative path constraints can be computed in polynomial time, and the almost-sure, as well as the positive winning set of zero-sum games with quantitative path constraints can be decided in quadratic time.

(1) qualitative determinacy results hold for mean-payoff games; (2) optimal strategy complexity for mean-payoff objectives is the same as for reachability objectives; and (3), for quantitative constraints, a polynomial time solution to the almost-sure winning problem for mean-payoff concurrent games would disprove the conjecture that the value problem for deterministic mean-payoff turn-based games is not solvable in polynomial-time.

(a) for qualitative constraints the problem of computing almost-sure and (b) positive winning sets can be solved in quadratic time, and (c) for quantitative constraints the problem of almost-sure and of positive winning sets can not be solved in polynomial time unless a long-standing open question is positively solved.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of determining the winner in concurrent games with limit-average payoff.

a general framework for solving turn-based zero-sum games: it generalizes the classical complexity results for turn-based deterministic mean payoff games, and includes other classical objectives as special cases.
a generalization of the fundamental problem of turn-based mean-payoff games to the case of concurrent games.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the qualitative mean-payoff and the quantitative mean-payoff problems for concurrent games are essentially equal, in the sense that the qualitative problem is computationally harder but has a similar decidability frontier as the quantitative problem, and they have the same computational complexity and almost identical algorithmic techniques.
the qualitative winning set for concurrent mean-payoff objective with almost-sure winning is computationally equivalent to turn-based deterministic mean pay-off games.

the qualitative complexity and the quantitative complexity of the almost-sures and positive winning sets are the same for concurrent mean-payoff game, but the quantitative complexity of these sets is unknown for turn-based mean-payoff games.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the qualitative winning properties for concurrent mean-payoff and turn-based mean-payoff games are computationally equivalent, and the qualitative and the quantitative properties for concurrent mean payoff games are co-NP complete.
the qualitative winning set problem for concurrent games with mean-payoff objectives is polynomially equivalent to the quantitative one.

the qualitative winning set for concurrent games can be solved in quadratic time, the quantitative winning set for concurrent mean-payoff can only be solved in worst-case exponential time, and a wide range of open problems are still wide open and qualitative analysis for concurrent mean-pay-off games has not been studied before.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in concurrent games the qualitative and quantitative problems are substantially more complex than in turn-based games.
in concurrent games the qualitative winning properties are computationally much more tractable than the quantitative ones.

while qualitative winning is a very natural objective for concurrent games that has been studied for years, it has not been formally addressed for concurrent games, and we show that it is significantly more complicated to handle than the quantitative objective of turn-based games.
